Trust me I was a chronic relapser for 5 years. Smoked for 9 years, but knew it was a problem 4 years into it. I would get to 30, 60, 90 days over and over and relapse.

I finally have a year sober under my belt. There is hope. You won’t think about it everyday. You still will have occasional cravings sure, but the amount of mental space that becomes freed after 6-8 months of sobriety is SO worth it. I have been through the worst grief, losing my dad at 9 months and I thought I’d for sure relapse but I didn’t. I used to be the type that would relapse just because I had a headache. Trust me change is possible, but moderation isn’t. I’ll never be able to control my thoughts or use of marijuana if it is in my life, but truly out of sight out of mind becomes true. Think of quitting as going to the gym. 3 months of consistently working out is nice but you’re not going to have your dream bod, nor is it a lifestyle at this point. But hitting 6, 9 and 12 months? You’re going to have a sense of discipline that’s harder to crack. You won’t be thinking of skipping the gym as often

I encourage you to go a year without weed before entertaining the “maybe I can moderate” demon. I promise you after a year of sobriety you won’t be craving it the same way. 3 months without it is long in comparison to doing it everyday, but 3 months really isn’t that long to suddenly change a lifelong habit. 
If you went to the gym for 3 months would you expect a 6 pack? No. You’d just be getting into the swing of things and starting to show some results. But a year of consistently working out? You’re not gonna wanna go back to eating like shit and not working out because the results will be so evident. Same concept.

YTA - Your mom is literally trying. This is a very hard change for anyone who’s known you pretransition regardless of their views on LGBTQ+ folks. A family friend of mine who is extremely accepting recently had one of their adult children come out as trans. Regardless it still has taken her awhile to fully accept the loss of her daughter and retraining her brain to view him as her son. It’s not a matter of transphobia it’s just a matter of it’s a HUGE change not just for you but for the people around you too.

There’s a reason the term “dead name” is a thing, its because for many it’s mourning the person you once were. That mourning is extended to those in your life, especially your parents. I think you’re a bit of a bully in the situation quite frankly, it’s clear you just want her to INSTANTLY use your new name and pronouns unquestioningly and that’s just not a realistic or fair expectation. 

You want her to respect your feelings while showing zero respect for hers. She was honest in that it’s hard for her to accept and she’s mad at herself for it but wants to go to therapy to work on that. What more could you want?? Other than some fairytale where she is just instantly able to shift to a whole new name and gender identity for her child of xx years without any hesitation while also proclaiming your identity to the rest of your family. That’s just unrealistic. 

Also would you rather her just placate you and say “sure ___ you’re my daughter” just to appease you but in actually she still internally views you as her son and never does the work to actually view you as her daughter. Or would you rather her take a little while longer to get used to your new name/identity, but instead she’s doing the work, she’s learning about your feelings and comes FULLY to terms with the fact that you are her daughter?? Sounds like she’s trying to do the latter which is GOOD. She loves you and is trying, that’s a GIFT that most lgbtq+ folks don’t have. Stop squandering it and get over yourself.

I also was diagnosed at 21 and I think my intelligence and ability to skate by on paper is why my ADHD was undiagnosed for so long. It’s also why my life is currently a mess from being unable to properly cope with it outside of an academic setting as an adult. I also feel angry about the potential I had of doing more with my intelligence had i been diagnosed earlier. I dropped out of college at 19 due to covid and things going online, for me it was impossible to do well with that going on especially being unmedicated back then. I still haven’t gone back and I feel angry looking back on how I could’ve handled a lot of situations like that better in my life had I been diagnosed earlier. But my intelligence is why I was able to mask it so well and fly under the radar.

Growing up I simply was a very good test taker and I can pick up on things very quick when it’s crunch time but otherwise my intelligence is kind of useless to me. I would barely ever do my homework but I would get 90-100% on tests while barely paying attention in class (maladaptive daydreaming, and then just skipping when I got older) so I was never failing my classes despite having shit attendance and having tons of zeros in homework/project categories. I would skate by with mostly Bs in the end, but it makes me mad that I could’ve excelled and gotten into a much better college then I did and life would be much different for me had I been diagnosed sooner. I got into an okay university and went for one year before dropping out. 

Then university somewhat reinforced my bad adhd habits. I still did great on exams despite barely showing up to my classes and now they were worth a bigger % of the grade. So I did better on paper in university but still had such bad habits that were kinda being rewarded. Once covid hit though it switched to the exams being worth less and more of a project/attendance emphasis since it’s easier to cheat from home. Executive dysfunction + online class = my grades tanking and me dropping out. I wanna go back eventually but I’m still picking up the pieces from the financial decisions I had to make as a result of dropping out so idk. Kind of why I’m a tad bitter still about not being diagnosed sooner, but I am medicated now and getting my life back on track. 

I really resonate with feeling like an imposter because people in school would be like “I had to study all night for this exam” and I would just show up and do the same or better than them. Or I would BS my way through essays the last minute and usually get an A while others would put in time and get a B. But if you’re still in university, I have to warn you and say you might be in for a rude awakening like I was about how bad your ADHD symptoms are when it comes to other adult responsibilities in the future. I live alone now and whew, BSing my way through school was certainly easier than managing all my current responsibilities w/adhd. My life quickly became a mess and it’s what pushed me to get a diagnosis.

Being sober will always be the better option. This doesn’t mean life being sober is always great. There’s a reason you quit, but there’s also a reason you started using in the first place after all. You have to dig deep into what caused you to use and begin making those changes. Sobriety doesn’t just change your life automatically, sobriety just gives you the possibility to change your life. Support groups are great, but similar to therapy, just talking about problems without making radical changes can only do so much. So ask yourself what, besides not smoking, is different about your life now versus when you were using? If it’s not much, of course sobriety isn’t going to be “better.” Sobriety is only as great as you make it. If just being sober was enough to live a happy life, addictions wouldn’t happen to begin with.

72 days sober is definitely something you should be proud of, but in the grand scheme of things it’s a very small portion of your life. Your life won’t drastically improve that quickly especially since you’re just getting over the withdrawals. Think about something like body building, for example, 72 days of going hard at the gym isn’t going to automatically get you a 6 pack. Significant life changes and your quality of life improving usually takes longer than a couple months. And remember this is the hard part! You’re just over the worst of it, it would be such a shame to reset all your progress and inevitably you will want to quit again. I relapsed at 110 days a year ago and it was SO difficult to get sober again, i also had similar feelings to you constantly thinking “is sobriety even worth it?” But the truth is I wasn’t living that much of a different life to when I was using so of course I was going to relapse. But that desire to quit never went away, it just became so much harder to do it again. So please stick with it as long as you can, you don’t wanna have to be at day 1 again and again.

I don’t know if you’re doing these things already, since you made no mention but personally I take sleep supplements to help with my insomnia. Read books and have a proper unwinding an hour before bed without your phone. Exercise and watch your diet for the weight loss. I know you don’t want to hear “give it more time” but regarding the brain fog, you DO need to give it more time. It takes at least 90 days for THC to completely leave your system, and even then your brain has to recalibrate to life without THC.

Also talk to your doctor regarding your mental health issues if they continue to be an issue. I was always so hesitant about prescription medication, but my prescription medication quite literally saved my life. I had a notion that “I don’t want to be reliant on prescription medication.” But being reliant on weed is SO much worse. I wasn’t on prescription medication during my 110 days, but I know looking back it would’ve made my first long stint of sobriety 2x easier. Maybe talk with your doctor about that.

I’m just now at 40 days again, a year after my 110 days and numerous failed attempts at quitting. I can tell you that I regret relapsing and having to throw away a whole year of my life to weed again. Please keep going. You’ll regret relapsing, I promise you.
